Best Black Friday Apple Watch deals so far: U.S.

  • Apple Watch Ultra 4: $699.99 ($99 off, MSRP $799) – already the best price we’ve seen

Best Black Friday Apple Watch deals so far: U.K.

  • Apple Watch Ultra 4: £729 (£20 off, RRP £749) – the best price we’ve seen so far
  • Apple Watch Ultra 3: £519 (£230 less than Apple Watch Ultra 4) – the best price we’ve seen

PRICES CHECKED 10 NOVEMBER, 2026 – Deals change quickly, so we will update this page throughout November

Black Friday is a great time to buy an Apple Watch, with retailers discounting everything from the affordable SE to the premium Ultra. Last year’s U.S. offers included $50 off the SE 3, up to $70 off the then-new Series 11, and $100 off the Ultra 3. Older models brought bigger savings, including $150 off the Series 10 and $200 off the Ultra 2. In the U.K., clearance offers were particularly attractive: the Series 10 was up to £130 off at Currys, while Argos cut £200 from the Ultra 2’s original price.

October Prime Day brought discounts on this year’s models, too. In the U.S., the 42mm Series 12 fell to $349, the 40mm SE 3 to $199, and the Ultra 4 to $774 – savings of $50, $50, and $25 respectively. U.K. highlights included the SE 3 at £199 and the previous-generation Series 11 at £259.

This Black Friday, we’d watch the Series 12 for discounts on our best Apple Watch for most people, the SE 3 for an affordable entry point, and the Ultra 4 for longer battery life and outdoor features. Remaining Series 11 and Ultra 3 stock could offer particularly good value if priced sufficiently below their replacements. Below, we explain which offers are worth taking and when to wait; for savings across Apple’s other products, see our best Apple Black Friday deals.

Which Apple Watch should you buy this Black Friday?

Apple Watch Series 12 – Our best overall choice

Apple

The Series 12 is the Apple Watch we recommend for most people. It combines Apple’s new Health Sensing System, more frequent heart-rate measurements, a Readiness score, and a tougher display with up to 24 hours of battery life.

A worthwhile Black Friday discount could make it an attractive purchase, but compare it with remaining Series 11 stock. The older model has the same quoted battery life, so a substantial saving may outweigh the newer health features.

U.S. Black Friday price: During October Prime Day, the 42mm GPS Series 12 fell to $349, while the 46mm version reached $399 – $50 off each. Last Black Friday, its predecessor, the Series 11, received discounts of up to $70. So far this Black Friday month we’ve seen prices drop by $9, but we expect they will drop further.

U.K. Black Friday price: We didn’t see Series 12 discounts during October Prime Day and so far this November there have been no price drops, but we are hopeful.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 – Best for battery life and outdoor adventures

Apple

The Ultra 4 is our choice for endurance athletes, outdoor enthusiasts, and buyers who prioritize battery life. It offers up to 50 hours of normal use, satellite communication, precision dual-frequency GPS, diving features, and Apple’s new Health Sensing System.

It’s more watch than most people need, but the current $699.99 offer is substantially below October Prime Day’s $774 price, making it worth considering if you want the latest Ultra. Compare it with the Ultra 3, though, which retains many of its outdoor features but has a shorter 42-hour battery-life rating.

U.S. Black Friday price: October Prime Day brought the Ultra 4 down to $774, a $25 saving. This November we’ve already seen the Apple Watch Ultra 4 for $699.99 on Amazon: that’s $99 off.

U.K. Black Friday price: The Ultra 4 remained at its full £749 price during October Prime Day, but we’ve already seen it drop by £20 to £729 at Amazon.

Apple Watch SE 3 – Our best budget choice

Apple / Amazon

The SE 3 is the best-value option for buyers who want the core Apple Watch experience. It includes an always-on display, temperature sensing, fast charging, and the S10 chip, but lacks ECG, blood oxygen monitoring, and the newer Health Sensing System.

It remains part of Apple’s current lineup despite launching in 2025. A strong Black Friday offer could make it an excellent affordable purchase, although its previous discounts mean there’s little reason to settle for a token reduction.

U.S. Black Friday price: Both last Black Friday and October Prime Day brought the 40mm GPS model to $199 and the 44mm version to $229—$50 below their regular prices. So far, the U.S. price drop is just $9 at Amazon, so we’d hold out for bigger savings.

U.K. Black Friday price: Black Friday 2025 and October Prime Day brought the 40mm GPS model to £199 and the 44mm version to £229, saving £20. So far we haven’t seen any price drops for Black Friday 2026.

Apple Watch Ultra 3 – Best clearance option for outdoor enthusiasts

Apple

The Ultra 3 is worth considering if you want a rugged Apple Watch without paying for the latest model. It offers satellite communication, dual-frequency GPS, diving features, and up to 42 hours of battery life.

You give up the Ultra 4’s longer battery life and newer Health Sensing System. Compare their actual selling prices: the Ultra 3 needs to be sufficiently cheaper to justify choosing the older generation.

U.S. Black Friday price: Last Black Friday, the Ultra 3 fell to $699, a $100 saving. Our October Prime Day coverage found only used models, so it didn’t identify a comparable new-stock offer. So far this November we’ve seen the Apple Watch Ultra 3 for $649, but that’s only $51 cheaper than the Ultra 4, so we’d favor the newer model.

U.K. Black Friday price: Last Black Friday, the Ultra 3 was £719, or £30 off. October Prime Day listed it at £569. The price is even lower this November – you can get it for £519 at Amazon, £230 less than the usual Apple Watch Ultra 4 price.

Apple Watch Series 11 – Best clearance option for everyday use

Apple Watch Series 11

The Series 11 could be a better-value everyday watch than the Series 12 if the price gap is large enough. It has the same quoted 24-hour battery life, although it misses the newer Health Sensing System and Audio Intelligence features.

For buyers who don’t need those additions, a substantial clearance discount could be more useful than a small saving on the latest model.

U.S. Black Friday price: Last Black Friday, the 42mm GPS Series 11 reached $339, while the 46mm version was $359 – savings of $60 and $70, respectively. Our October Prime Day coverage found only used models in the U.S. and so far that’s all we are seeing this November.

U.K. Black Friday price: October Prime Day brought the 42mm Series 11 to £259 and the 46mm version to £299. Last Black Friday’s bigger clearance offers were on the preceding Series 10, which was available for £279 in 42mm and £299 in 46mm. In November 2026 you can get a Series 11 for £299, £120 less than the equivalent Series 12.

Should you buy an Apple Watch now or wait for a better deal?

With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need an Apple Watch immediately. But sales stretch across much of November, so you don’t necessarily need to wait for Black Friday itself. If an early offer matches or comes close to a previous low for the same model and configuration, it can be worth taking – particularly if you want a specific size, color, or band combination.

October Prime Day prices provide useful benchmarks. In the U.S., the Series 12 fell to $349 for the 42mm GPS model and $399 for the 46mm version, while the Ultra 4 reached $774. The SE 3 was $199 in 40mm and $229 in 44mm. Those SE prices also appeared last Black Friday, so we’d look for offers matching or beating them. In the U.K., October highlights included the 40mm SE 3 at £199 and the older 42mm Series 11 at £259.

The Series 12 and Ultra 4 only arrived in September, so finding a better price is the main reason to wait. If you don’t need a watch immediately, those previous offers give you a useful starting point for deciding whether to buy now or hold out.

Compare retailers, too. Last Black Friday, Walmart offered $150 off the Series 10, while U.K. shoppers could find up to £130 off at Currys and £200 off the Ultra 2’s original price at Argos. Our guide to the best time to buy an Apple Watch has more advice on choosing when to purchase.

Should you buy an older Apple Watch?

David Price / Foundry

Don’t assume an older Apple Watch is a bad buy. The Series 11 and Ultra 3 are only one generation old and can make excellent purchases if they’re substantially cheaper than the Series 12 or Ultra 4. Both retain many of their replacements’ core features, although you miss the newer Health Sensing System and, with the Ultra 3, the Ultra 4’s longer battery life.

Compare actual selling prices, matching case size, material, connectivity, and band where possible. A $50 difference between a Series 11 and Series 12 may not be enough to justify giving up the newer model’s health features, whereas a substantially larger saving could change the calculation. A discounted Series 11 could also be worth considering alongside the SE 3 if a small premium gets you features you’ll use.

Be much more cautious with the Series 8, SE 2, and original Ultra: those models cannot run watchOS 27. The Series 9 is the oldest standard Apple Watch compatible with the latest software, while the Ultra 2 is the oldest supported Ultra and the SE 3 is the only supported SE. Missing the latest software doesn’t make an older watch unusable, but it makes it harder to recommend as a purchase today.

The Series 9, Series 10, and Ultra 2 can still be worth considering at sufficiently low prices. However, compatibility with today’s software doesn’t guarantee how many future upgrades they’ll receive. Weigh the savings against the watch’s age and features, rather than assuming every supported generation offers equally good value.

Apple Watch deals to avoid

David Price / Foundry

Don’t let a bigger advertised discount tempt you into paying more for a cellular Apple Watch you won’t use. If your iPhone is usually nearby, a GPS model can already handle calls, messages, and notifications through your phone. It can also track runs, use Apple Pay, and play downloaded music without your iPhone. As our experience testing a cellular Apple Watch showed, the extra connectivity may add little to everyday use.

Cellular is worth considering if you regularly leave your iPhone behind and want to remain contactable without Wi-Fi, or you’re setting up a watch for a child without an iPhone. Otherwise, you could pay extra for the hardware and then add an ongoing mobile-plan charge for a feature you rarely need. You don’t have to activate a plan on a cellular model, so it can still be a good buy if its sale price matches or beats the GPS version. Apple scandals usually revolve around a piece of hardware failing to do what it’s supposed to do: a phone, for instance, that loses connection, or bends in the pocket, or breaks when used normally. So the latest controversy is at least refreshingly different, in that hardware is barely involved at all.

For a couple of weeks now the consumer rights advocate Louis Rossman has been reporting on allegations of malpractice in Apple stores. (You can catch the gist in his latest video on the topic, while a fuller exploration is given in this earlier video.) It’s alleged, specifically, that multiple retail employees in multiple stores have signed up customers to auto-renewing subscription services without obtaining fully informed consent. And worse, that an employee performance metric put in place by Apple management incentivized them to do so.

Apple stores have a system called Connect and Personalize, under which purchasers of a new iPhone, iPad, or Mac scan a QR code to receive a tutorial from a retail employee. This process temporarily unlocks the customer’s account and payment information and shows the employee any free subscription trials for which the customer is eligible. Look, they will then say, you can get three months of Apple One (for example) for free; tap here to start your trial.

Like most services companies, Apple offers free trials not out of a sense of altruism but in the hopes that customers will carry on using the service after the trial ends. They are free to start with, then they auto-renew after a certain amount of time and the customer begins to pay. But whistleblowers claim the auto-renewal part of the deal was not always made clear to customers. Some employees implied that the trials were simply a gift with no strings; others, it is alleged, tapped Accept on their own device and didn’t get consent at all. Needless to say these are very serious allegations. We have contacted Apple for comment and will update this article to include the company’s response if we receive one.

While reports claim the practice is or has been relatively widespread (one tipster told Rossman that they had “confirmed with others that this happens at other stores” and that “many employees [have] admit[ted] to me that they do this”), one defense Apple could offer is that these were rogue employees taking matters into their own hands. That it wasn’t company policy to have employees behave in this way, and that company management is indeed aghast to hear about such goings-on.

But the issue with that defense is that the problem appears to be systemic. Not explicitly, and perhaps not intentionally, but indirectly as a result of employee incentives.

Apple, again like other companies, tracks the performance of its retail employees. Until recently, one metric by which performance was graded was called “services attach rate:” the percentage of device purchasers assisted by the employee who signed up for a subscription service. It’s been reported that employees in at least some stores were set a target of 40 percent. If you help 10 people buy iPads, you should make sure at least four of them sign up to something at the same time.

It isn’t clear what action was taken (or threatened) against employees who failed to meet this target, or whether there was a reward for those who did. But targets affect behavior even in the absence of explicit punishments and rewards. The mere existence of that 40 percent figure tells employees that the company values that specific form of success, and heavily implies that success or failure by this metric will be one of the factors used to determine promotions, redundancies, pay raises, and bonuses. It would be surreally naive to imagine that putting in place a target of this nature wouldn’t encourage employees to hard-sell signups and, in at least a few cases across an organization with more than 100,000 retail staff, bend the rules regarding informed consent.

Apple stopped tracking services attach rate shortly after Rossman’s reporting was published. This might be taken as a tacit acknowledgement that the metric was a bad idea with the potential to incentivise unethical behavior, but Apple claims it’s actually just a coincidence; the company told MacRumors the metric is simply “less relevant during the holiday season.” If that is truly the case, no doubt the metric will be reinstated in the new year.

The company has also reportedly sent internal memos to retail stores reminding employees to make sure they obtain informed consent before signing up customers to subscription trials, and to ensure it is customers, not the employees themselves, tapping the buttons. Again, this may or may not be a coincidence. Stores hire lots of new staff for the holiday season. Maybe it’s just a reminder for the newbies. But the timing is striking, to say the least.

Abuse the user: The dark side of services

Apple’s relentless march into services was one of the great successes of the Tim Cook era.

Overly dependent on the iPhone and trying to plan for the eventual decline of the smartphone market, the company pivoted: instead of just selling hardware, it would focus more and more on selling subscription services to people who own the hardware. This leads to steadier, more predictable recurring revenue and (assuming you own the services content, which Apple does wherever possible) effortless scalability. Building six million iPhone Duos is very difficult and expensive. Making one motor-racing movie is quite difficult and expensive, but distributing it to six million people barely increases your costs at all. At first glance it looks like a business model that’s all upside.

Services certainly have their advantages, and they’ve helped put Apple in a spectacularly strong financial position: this category brought in $30 billion of revenue in the last quarter alone. But selling subscriptions is a murkier business than selling one-off hardware purchases, because there’s more of a disconnect between the best outcomes for buyer and seller.

Selling hardware is essentially a collaborative effort, where both seller and buyer want the same thing: for the buyer to be pleased about the quality of the product and then buy the next model a year or two down the line. Sure, it’s a bit more complicated than that. We could talk about planned obsolescence, and unscrupulous retail employees encouraging people to buy a more powerful model than they need–although in both cases, short-term gain for the seller would come at the risk of long-term loss of user goodwill. In any case, because it’s a single purchase, the dynamic is relatively simple.

But when you switch to services, the best outcomes become radically decoupled. When it comes to streaming, for example, it’s clearly in the best interests of the customer to shop around, unsubscribe regularly, take a month of Netflix here and a month of Apple TV there. But it’s in the streamer’s interest for you to sign up and forget about it, like a gym owner who loses interest in your fitness journey the second you join. This is why whole seasons being dumped at once (which is good for the user) has largely been replaced by weekly drops, which is better for the streaming company.

If you pay for an iCloud+ subscription, similarly, your hope is that the storage allocation will prove adequate for your needs. Apple would much rather have your needs subtly increase, pushing you up to the next tier. If you pay for Apple Music, the company would ideally like for sharing to be a problem so you have to pay for the Family plan. Apple hasn’t yet put ads in these services, but (based on past behavior) it’s plausible that at some point it will follow the lead of Netflix and others and make the cheapest tier of TV+, Music, and Fitness+ ad-supported, thereby ensuring additional revenue while pushing customers to pay more for a higher tier.

Services, in short, reward companies which deliver a user-hostile experience.

An opportunity to be better

Apple has been making and selling tech hardware for 50 years; Apple Music didn’t open until 2015. So, when it comes to services, the company has had far less of a chance to forge an identity.

This, then, is an opportunity. Just as it did in desktops, laptops, music players and smartphones, Apple can establish itself as the services company that’s different. The one that begins with the idea of a great user experience and then extrapolates from that, rather than just doing whatever scrapes the most data or boosts engagement or increases short-term revenue.

Goodness knows there’s plenty of public discontent with the practices of streaming companies. There are swathes of streamers out there crying out for a provider which doesn’t constantly put up prices, deluge the user with unskippable adverts, remove content without warning, and cancel shows without giving them a chance. That could be Apple. It could also be the one company which doesn’t get flack for making it easy to sign up to a subscription and incredibly hard to end one.

Instead, many customers’ first experience with Apple as a services company is going into a store, paying a small fortune for a product, and then getting pushed into signing up to a subscription they don’t want or need. As first impressions go, it’s hard to think of a worse one. Be better, Apple.

After two years, Apple will finally start shipping its new generation of Apple TV 4K this week, and while it comes with some nice improvements — like a faster chip — there’s something else that made headlines. The new model is much more expensive than the previous model, now starting at $299. Yes, there’s a lot to like about the new Apple TV. But while Apple has made its streaming box better, I’m not convinced the product is heading in the right direction.

Don’t get me wrong. I’ve always liked Apple’s set-top box. In fact, I think tvOS has one of the best interfaces of any streaming platform. But instead of making the Apple TV more accessible to more people, Apple keeps adding more powerful hardware and charging more for it. The problem is, most people don’t really need that power, and Apple itself doesn’t even take full advantage of it.

Does Apple TV really need all that power?

The main upgrade in the new Apple TV 4K is the A19 chip — the same one found in the iPhone 17. Benchmarks show a 50 percent gain in CPU speed and double the graphics performance between the new chip and the A15 from the previous Apple TV. That’s an impressive leap, but the thing is, do you really need all that power just to watch TV?

Most people who own an Apple TV don’t use it for much more than watching movies and TV shows. Apps like Netflix, YouTube, or even Apple TV don’t need that much power. Even if you occasionally use AirPlay or play a light game from Apple Arcade, you probably won’t have any performance issues with older Apple TV models. Sure, the A19 brings some meaningful improvements, including more efficient video decoding, but I find it hard to believe that most people will notice this upgrade on an Apple TV.

Even Apple is having a hard time justifying the upgrade. In the press release announcing the new Apple TV 4K, it says that the A19 chip enables “greater responsiveness, faster navigation, and smoother animations.” That doesn’t sound convincing enough to me to buy a new Apple TV. I’m all for making a product faster, but there’s a point where adding more power stops making a meaningful difference to the experience.

What about Intel Macs?

macOS 27 marks another major step in Apple’s transition away from Intel. macOS 26 Tahoe was the final version to support Intel Macs, and Apple is now encouraging developers to remove Intel code from their apps and focus on Apple silicon.

macOS 27 will also be the final version to support Rosetta, Apple’s translation technology for running Intel-only apps on Apple silicon Macs. Those apps will continue to work in macOS 27, but will stop working in macOS 28 unless developers release Apple silicon-native versions.

To help users prepare, macOS 27 includes an Intel-app checker in System Settings that lists Intel-based apps used during the past year. If you still rely on any essential Intel-only software, now is a good time to look for updates or alternatives before upgrading to macOS 28.

What happens to DVD support?

macOS 27 also begins the phase-out of Apple’s native DVD support. Apple has removed the DVDPlayback framework from the macOS 27 SDK and says it will disappear completely in a future version of macOS.

Golden Gate may still include the DVD Player app, but it is likely to be the last macOS release with Apple’s built-in DVD playback support. Users who still watch DVDs on a Mac will increasingly need to rely on third-party software such as VLC.

Will macOS 27 support Rosetta and Intel apps?

macOS 27 will run Intel-only Mac apps through Rosetta 2. However, macOS 27 will be the final version of macOS to support Rosetta 2 as a general-purpose translation technology for running Intel-based Mac apps on Apple silicon.

Rosetta has acted as a transition layer since Apple introduced its own Mac chips in 2020, translating x86_64 Intel instructions so older software can run on Apple silicon. After macOS 27, most Intel-only Mac apps will no longer work unless developers release Apple silicon-native versions, although Apple will retain limited Rosetta functionality for some older, unmaintained games.

Apple is already preparing users for the change. Since macOS 26.4, Macs can display warnings when launching apps that rely on Rosetta, encouraging users (and the app developers) to update to Apple silicon-native versions before general Rosetta support ends.

These include:

  • Black or missing desktop previews: A black screen may appear when switching Spaces.

Siri AI: Siri powered macOS 27 features

Foundry

Apple’s biggest focus in macOS 27 Golden Gate is Siri AI, a completely redesigned version of Siri powered by Apple Intelligence. Rather than functioning primarily as a voice assistant, Siri is now a conversational AI that can answer questions, understand personal and onscreen context, access current information from the web and take actions across apps.

Siri AI behaves more like a generative-AI chatbot than the Siri of old. It can answer questions directly, understand natural follow-ups and solve problems instead of simply directing users to web searches.

At a glance: What’s new with Siri AI?

  • Conversational AI assistant: Siri can handle open-ended questions, brainstorming, research and natural back-and-forth conversations.
  • Dedicated Siri app: A standalone Siri app keeps conversations in one place and syncs them through iCloud, allowing users to start a conversation on one Apple device and continue it on another.
  • Personal context awareness: Siri can understand information in Messages, Mail, Notes, Photos, Maps and files to locate information and provide answers based on your personal data.
  • Web-powered answers: Siri can access current information from the web, making it more useful for research, learning, interview preparation and questions about recent events.
  • App actions and automation: Siri can perform tasks across apps such as Messages, Music, Reminders, Calendar and Maps using natural-language instructions.
  • Spotlight integration: Siri AI is integrated with Spotlight, allowing users to type questions and receive AI-generated answers without opening a browser or separate app.
  • Visual Intelligence: Visual Intelligence comes to the Mac for the first time, allowing Siri to understand selected images, documents, files, text and other content displayed on screen.

Macwelt

  • Writing Tools: Siri can generate text, rewrite drafts, summarise content and adjust wording or tone. Apple says it can also adapt writing to the way you typically communicate with particular contacts.
  • Improved dictation: Systemwide dictation gains better speech recognition along with automatic punctuation, capitalization and formatting.
  • Custom Siri voices: Users can choose Siri’s voice and adjust characteristics such as pace and expressiveness, although some of these capabilities require newer hardware.

A Siri AI contextural popover was discovered during beta testing. Selecting text brings up a small Siri icon offering contextual actions, including Writing Tools, summaries and key points, sending messages or emails, creating calendar events, opening locations in Maps, and tracking flights or packages. However, the feature is not enabled by default and requires Apple’s FeatureFlags system to activate. It remains unclear whether Apple intends to make it available as a consumer-facing feature.

Apple also appears to be taking a relatively restrained approach to AI behaviour. In our testing, Siri avoids presenting itself as human, excessive flattery and potentially harmful responses, while generally keeping its answers straightforward.

Siri AI has launched as a beta, so users should expect some rough edges and continued improvements.

With macOS 27.2, Siri AI supports French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish in addition to English. Availability will vary by region. Siri AI is available on Mac and Vision Pro in the European Union, although Siri AI remains unavailable on iPhone and iPad in the EU at launch because of issues related to the Digital Markets Act. It is also unavailable in mainland China while Apple works through regulatory requirements.

Which Macs support Siri AI?

Siri AI requires a Mac that supports Apple Intelligence, but some of its most advanced capabilities have higher hardware requirements. Apple says its most powerful on-device AI model, expressive Siri voices and advanced dictation require an M3 or later Mac with at least 12GB of unified memory. Macs that support Apple Intelligence but do not meet those requirements can still receive other Siri AI features, although the exact feature set may vary.

Apple

  • Notify Me: Safari can monitor webpages for changes and alert you when something happens, such as a product coming back in stock or a price dropping, removing the need to keep refreshing pages manually.

  • Faster, more efficient browsing: Apple says Safari uses less power while improving page-loading speed, JavaScript performance, scrolling, animations and resizing of the Start Page.

Messages

Passwords

Parental Controls

Apple expands its family-safety tools with Safari’s Ask to Browse, improved Screen Time and Time Allowances, contact approvals, and broader Communication Safety protections. The changes give parents more control over what children can access and who they can communicate with without completely locking down the Mac.

The redesigned parental controls also have a family-wide software requirement. To activate them through Family Sharing, every eligible device in the group – not just the parent’s Mac – must be running iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27 or visionOS 27.

Once Apple offers the migration, the family organizer or a parent or guardian should see a Get Started prompt in Family settings. Apple says parents can also select the child’s name under System Settings > Family to begin setup, although the migration options are not currently appearing for everyone.

Older devices that cannot install version 27 can continue using the previous Screen Time and Family Sharing controls. Accessibility, Shared Albums and Suggestions

macOS 27 also includes accessibility improvements, expanded Shared Albums, and more contextual Suggestions throughout the operating system.

Game Porting Toolkit 4

Apple’s Game Porting Toolkit 4 arrives alongside macOS 27 and promises significant improvements for running and porting Windows games on Apple silicon Macs. Early beta testing suggests substantial performance gains. On an M4 Pro MacBook Pro, GTA V reportedly increased from around 106fps to 176fps, while Red Dead Redemption 2 improved from roughly 60fps to 75fps.

The results suggest software compatibility, rather than raw Apple silicon performance, is increasingly the main obstacle to better Mac gaming. Improvements to Game Porting Toolkit could make Windows titles more practical to run and easier for developers to bring to macOS.

Design and Interface Changes in macOS 27

Apple

macOS 27 Golden Gate refines the Liquid Glass redesign introduced in macOS 26, with Apple focusing on readability, consistency and usability rather than another major visual overhaul.

Changes include:

  • Improved Liquid Glass: Stronger contrast, better readability and more consistent refraction effects across windows, menus and controls.
  • Customizable transparency: Users can adjust the Liquid Glass effect in System Settings, from a clearer appearance to a more heavily tinted look.
  • Cleaner Finder and toolbars: Finder sidebars are more clearly defined, toolbars are more consistent, and edge-to-edge sidebars replace some of the floating elements introduced in macOS 26.
  • More consistent windows: Window corners, controls and active-window highlighting have been standardized to make the interface feel more coherent.
  • Updated icons and menus: Menu-bar and app icons gain sharper outlines, improved contrast and more depth, while unnecessary menu icons have been reduced.
  • Smoother window management: Mission Control and Spaces animations have been refined, and active windows should be easier to distinguish.
  • New wallpapers and screensavers: Golden Gate-themed backgrounds include animated daytime and nighttime views of the bridge.
  • Swipe to refresh: Supported Mac apps gain a swipe-down-to-refresh gesture.
  • Improved iPhone Mirroring: iPhone Mirroring adds Control Center access, resizable app windows and support for DRM-protected video.

Touch on Mac: How macOS works with a touchscreen

macOS 27 supports direct touchscreen input on the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. Touch works alongside the keyboard and trackpad, giving you another way to interact with apps rather than replacing the controls you already use.

You can swipe to scroll through webpages, pinch to zoom into photos, and drag content between documents. Window gestures include double-tapping to fill the screen and flicking a window to tile it into place. Apple says many existing apps work immediately because macOS translates touches into mouse clicks, while developers can use updated gesture APIs to build more specialized touch controls.

Apple has also announced touch-focused updates for creative apps. Examples include playing onscreen instruments in Logic Pro and selecting ranges, placing clips and zooming into edits in Final Cut Pro. These app updates are scheduled for November.

Direct touchscreen input requires compatible hardware: the 14-inch or 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

Performance improvements and system changes in macOS 27

Apple says macOS 27 focuses on speed, efficiency and everyday usability, with improvements across apps, networking, displays and system tasks. Most of these changes do not require Apple Intelligence.

Changes include:

  • Faster overall performance: Apps should launch more quickly, while an optimized CPU scheduler improves system responsiveness.
  • Faster Spotlight and setup: Spotlight indexing and new user-account creation are quicker.
  • Faster file transfers and networking: AirDrop and network file browsing are faster, while Ethernet status can appear in the menu bar.
  • Thunderbolt and Bluetooth improvements: RDMA over Thunderbolt has been improved, alongside more efficient Bluetooth power management.
  • Faster Safari: The Safari Start Page loads more quickly, with broader browser performance improvements.
  • Better external-display support: New high-resolution and high-refresh-rate modes include 5K at 120Hz, alongside improved display-position persistence, HDR support for the macOS interface and 5K Mac mirroring.

Apple Intelligence powered changes:

  • AI-powered file naming – requires Apple Intelligence: macOS can suggest filenames and folder names based on their contents, including in Pages, Numbers, TextEdit and Finder.
  • Systemwide proofreading – requires Apple Intelligence: Apple Intelligence provides automatic proofreading and improved spelling and grammar suggestions throughout macOS.

Apple Intelligence privacy: Apple says AI processing happens on-device where possible, with Private Cloud Compute used for more demanding tasks. Data processed in the cloud is not stored or made accessible to Apple.

  • MacBook Air (Apple silicon, 2020 and later)
  • MacBook Pro (Apple silicon, 2020 and later)
  • iMac (Apple silicon, 2021 and later)
  • Mac mini (Apple silicon, 2020 and later)
  • Mac Studio (2022 and later)
  • Mac Pro (Apple silicon, 2023 and later)

All supported Macs can run Apple Intelligence, although some of the most advanced Siri AI features require an M3 or later Mac with at least 12GB of unified memory.

What about Intel Macs?

macOS 27 marks another major step in Apple’s transition away from Intel. macOS 26 Tahoe was the final version to support Intel Macs, and Apple is now encouraging developers to remove Intel code from their apps and focus on Apple silicon.

macOS 27 will also be the final version to support Rosetta, Apple’s translation technology for running Intel-only apps on Apple silicon Macs. Those apps will continue to work in macOS 27, but will stop working in macOS 28 unless developers release Apple silicon-native versions.

To help users prepare, macOS 27 includes an Intel-app checker in System Settings that lists Intel-based apps used during the past year. If you still rely on any essential Intel-only software, now is a good time to look for updates or alternatives before upgrading to macOS 28.

What happens to DVD support?

macOS 27 also begins the phase-out of Apple’s native DVD support. Apple has removed the DVDPlayback framework from the macOS 27 SDK and says it will disappear completely in a future version of macOS.

Golden Gate may still include the DVD Player app, but it is likely to be the last macOS release with Apple’s built-in DVD playback support. Users who still watch DVDs on a Mac will increasingly need to rely on third-party software such as VLC.

Should Intel Mac owners upgrade now?

Intel Mac owners should start planning a move to Apple silicon, particularly if they want macOS 27, Apple Intelligence or continued access to the latest Mac features. The transition away from Intel hardware has reached a critical turning point, with software support rapidly vanishing and a new generation of affordable entry-level hardware making the switch more accessible than ever.

Apple has confirmed that macOS 27 will not support any Intel-based Macs. While a small number of Intel models may receive security patches for older versions of macOS until September 2028, they are already excluded from modern flagship features.

Those with Intel Macs also miss out on many features, including Apple Intelligence.

5.

Will macOS 27 support Rosetta and Intel apps?

macOS 27 will run Intel-only Mac apps through Rosetta 2. However, macOS 27 will be the final version of macOS to support Rosetta 2 as a general-purpose translation technology for running Intel-based Mac apps on Apple silicon.

Rosetta has acted as a transition layer since Apple introduced its own Mac chips in 2020, translating x86_64 Intel instructions so older software can run on Apple silicon. After macOS 27, most Intel-only Mac apps will no longer work unless developers release Apple silicon-native versions, although Apple will retain limited Rosetta functionality for some older, unmaintained games.

Apple is already preparing users for the change. Since macOS 26.4, Macs can display warnings when launching apps that rely on Rosetta, encouraging users (and the app developers) to update to Apple silicon-native versions before general Rosetta support ends.

In macOS 28, most Intel-only apps will no longer run unless developers update them for Apple silicon.

Should you buy an old pair of AirPods?

Older-generation AirPods can be a good buy at the right clearance price. Compare their actual selling price with the discounted price of their replacement, rather than focusing on the percentage saving from an old launch price. A substantial discount can make an older pair worthwhile; a small difference may leave you sacrificing useful features for little saving.

AirPods 4 are harder to recommend now that AirPods 5 include Active Noise Cancellation as standard, starting at the same $129 price previously charged for AirPods 4 without ANC. Check which AirPods 4 version you’re buying—there were models with and without noise cancellation—and look for a substantial saving over AirPods 5.

AirPods Pro 2 remain worth considering if they’re significantly cheaper than Pro 3. However, the newer model improves fit, noise cancellation, and battery life, while adding heart-rate sensing. Compare their sale prices carefully: a strong Pro 3 discount could make the older pair’s clearance offer less attractive.

The original AirPods Max also need a substantial discount to justify choosing them over Max 2. The newer headphones add the H2 chip, improved noise cancellation, and features including Adaptive Audio and Conversation Awareness. Check the generation rather than relying on the charging port alone: the original AirPods Max were also sold in a USB-C version.

Buying older stock new is different from buying used or refurbished AirPods. For those pairs, check the stated condition, charging case, warranty, and returns policy, and buy from a reputable seller. Be cautious about battery condition and unusually low marketplace prices, since convincing counterfeits can resemble genuine AirPods. Our guide explains how to spot fake AirPods.

Check whether the listing is for a new, refurbished, or used pair. For used or refurbished AirPods, look for clear information about condition, warranty, and returns coverage. Battery condition deserves particular caution: a low purchase price may be less attractive if listening time has deteriorated.

Compare retailers, too. Amazon isn’t always cheapest: Walmart and Best Buy also compete on AirPods pricing, while Argos offered competitive U.K. deals last year. Our guide to the best time to buy AirPods has more advice on purchase timing.

Should you buy an old pair of AirPods?

Older-generation AirPods can be a good buy at the right clearance price. Compare their actual selling price with the discounted price of their replacement, rather than focusing on the percentage saving from an old launch price. A substantial discount can make an older pair worthwhile; a small difference may leave you sacrificing useful features for little saving.

AirPods 4 are harder to recommend now that AirPods 5 include Active Noise Cancellation as standard, starting at the same $129 price previously charged for AirPods 4 without ANC. Check which AirPods 4 version you’re buying—there were models with and without noise cancellation—and look for a substantial saving over AirPods 5.

AirPods Pro 2 remain worth considering if they’re significantly cheaper than Pro 3. However, the newer model improves fit, noise cancellation, and battery life, while adding heart-rate sensing. Compare their sale prices carefully: a strong Pro 3 discount could make the older pair’s clearance offer less attractive.

The original AirPods Max also need a substantial discount to justify choosing them over Max 2. The newer headphones add the H2 chip, improved noise cancellation, and features including Adaptive Audio and Conversation Awareness. Check the generation rather than relying on the charging port alone: the original AirPods Max were also sold in a USB-C version.

Buying older stock new is different from buying used or refurbished AirPods. For those pairs, check the stated condition, charging case, warranty, and returns policy, and buy from a reputable seller. Be cautious about battery condition and unusually low marketplace prices, since convincing counterfeits can resemble genuine AirPods. Our guide explains how to spot fake AirPods.

AirPods deals to avoid

Foundry

Check exactly what an offer includes before comparing prices. Different charging-case packages can affect features and value, so make sure you’re comparing equivalent versions. Also check any spending requirements, contracts, or rebates attached to offers advertising “free” AirPods.

Judge the price against previous selling prices as well as the advertised discount. A large saving from the recommended retail price doesn’t necessarily mean a particularly good deal if retailers regularly charge less.

Check whether the listing is for a new, refurbished, or used pair. For used or refurbished AirPods, look for clear information about condition, warranty, and returns coverage. Battery condition deserves particular caution: a low purchase price may be less attractive if listening time has deteriorated.

Finally, check who is selling and dispatching your order, particularly when shopping through a marketplace. Unusually low prices from unfamiliar sellers warrant caution, since counterfeit AirPods can look convincing. Our guide explains how to tell if AirPods are fake.

How we choose AirPods deals

Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on AirPods reviews. We consider sound quality, noise cancellation, comfort, battery life, and everyday use – not just the specifications or advertised saving.

Our testing helps us explain which features are worth paying for. For example, our AirPods Pro 3 review assessed how securely the redesigned ear tips stayed in place during exercise, checked battery life against Apple’s claims, and evaluated the heart-rate sensor. Our AirPods Max 2 review weighed their excellent sound and noise cancellation against drawbacks including weight and the Smart Case.

Siri AI is just the beginning. According to the latest newsletter from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, who is always dialed-in to the inner workings of Apple, the new CEO John Ternus is pushing to make Apple a bigger player in the AI space.

While he had great things to say publicly about Siri AI at the launch of iOS 27, he is apparently delivering a somewhat different message in private. He seems aware, Gurman said, of the fact that Apple’s AI offerings are far behind rivals and not moving ahead with the same urgency. In a closed-door meeting with Craig Federighi, Ternus pushed to accelerate the company’s roadmap and move quickly past the long-overdue improvements to Siri.

With the OS 27.3 updates, developers will finally be able to make their apps accessible to Siri, so that Siri can perform in-app actions and access their data, if desired. Along with on-screen awareness and personal context, it’s the final pillar of the advanced capabilities Apple first announced two years ago.

But the latest trend in AI is agents. What started with hobbyist software like OpenClaw has grown into consumer-ready products like Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s Claude Duet. These AI agents run continuously and somewhat autonomously, taking care of almost anything a person can do online or on their phone or computer. There are some concerns over privacy and safety, and rightfully so, but they have already proven to be very popular.

That is a big step beyond “tell Siri to take actions within apps” and it’s where Ternus would like to take things. Gurman said Apple could make Siri act more like an autonomous agent “as early as next year,” and notes that the company hardly has a choice–announcing such a major feature at WWDC in June would put Apple a year behind the principal players else in the AI space, at least.

Gurman’s report paints the picture of a CEO concerned not just with matching AI companies feature-for-feature, but recognizing the increasing role of AI in computer use in general. The general idea is that, over time, more of what we do on our computing devices will be handled not by typing, clicking, and swiping, but by a personal agent that can essentially use any software we want it to at our direction. If you’re a company like Apple whose strength comes from selling physical computing devices and creating the operating systems that runs on them, ceding that level of control to a rival company could be an existential threat.
